title: Introductory Plant Physiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Introductory Plant Physiology curriculum: water relations, mineral nutrition, photosynthesis, respiration, translocation, plant growth hormones, tropisms and photoperiodism.

questions.question: Osmosis is defined as the movement of:
options: Water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential across a semi-permeable membrane
Solute molecules from high to low concentration across any membrane
Water against a water potential gradient using ATP
Gases from high to low pressure
questions.correct_answer: Water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential across a semi-permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, moving from higher to lower water potential.

questions.question: Water potential of a plant cell is the sum of which two main component potentials?
options: Matric potential and gravitational potential only
questions.correct_answer: Solute (osmotic) potential and pressure (turgor) potential
questions.explanation: Cell water potential is largely determined by the solute potential (always negative, due to dissolved solutes) and the pressure potential exerted by the cell wall against the protoplast.

questions.question: A plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution will lose water and its protoplast will shrink away from the cell wall, a phenomenon called:
questions.correct_answer: Plasmolysis
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic (strongly solute-concentrated) external solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis, causing the protoplast to shrink from the wall, i.e., plasmolysis.

questions.question: Turgor pressure in plant cells is important because it:
options: Provides mechanical rigidity to non-woody tissues and drives cell expansion
Prevents any water from entering the cell
Causes permanent shrinkage of the cell
questions.correct_answer: Provides mechanical rigidity to non-woody tissues and drives cell expansion
questions.explanation: Turgor pressure, generated as the protoplast pushes against the cell wall, keeps herbaceous tissue rigid, drives cell elongation and is central to stomatal guard cell movement.

questions.question: According to the cohesion-tension theory, water rises in the xylem of tall trees mainly due to:
options: Transpirational pull combined with cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls
Active pumping by living xylem cells
Root pressure alone, even in tall trees
questions.correct_answer: Transpirational pull combined with cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls
questions.explanation: Evaporation from leaf surfaces creates tension that pulls a continuous, cohesive water column up through the xylem, aided by adhesion of water to the vessel/tracheid walls.

questions.question: Transpiration occurs predominantly through:
questions.correct_answer: Stomata on the leaf surface
questions.explanation: Although some water is lost through the cuticle and lenticels, the vast majority of transpirational water loss occurs through open stomata.

questions.question: Guttation, seen as water droplets at leaf tips/margins in the early morning, results from:
options: Root pressure forcing xylem sap out through hydathodes when transpiration is low
Condensation of atmospheric water vapour on the leaf surface
Active secretion of water by stomata
questions.correct_answer: Root pressure forcing xylem sap out through hydathodes when transpiration is low
questions.explanation: When soil is moist and humidity is high (transpiration minimal), root pressure pushes xylem sap out through specialised pores called hydathodes, producing guttation droplets.

questions.question: Stomatal opening is primarily driven by:
options: Increased turgor pressure in guard cells due to potassium ion influx and accompanying water uptake
Loss of chlorophyll in guard cells
Increased turgor in the surrounding epidermal cells only
Direct light absorption by the stomatal pore itself
questions.correct_answer: Increased turgor pressure in guard cells due to potassium ion influx and accompanying water uptake
questions.explanation: Light-driven proton pumping causes K+ influx into guard cells, lowering their water potential, so water enters, increasing turgor and causing the guard cells to bow open the pore.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a macronutrient essential for plant growth?
questions.correct_answer: Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is required in relatively large quantities (a macronutrient) as a component of amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll, unlike micronutrients such as zinc, manganese and boron needed in trace amounts.

questions.question: A deficiency of nitrogen in plants typically manifests as:
options: Chlorosis (yellowing) starting in older leaves and stunted growth
Purple discolouration of leaf margins only
Death of the shoot apex only
questions.correct_answer: Chlorosis (yellowing) starting in older leaves and stunted growth
questions.explanation: Since nitrogen is mobile within the plant, it is remobilised from older leaves to younger tissue under deficiency, causing older leaves to yellow first, along with overall stunted growth.

questions.question: Magnesium is a component of which vital plant molecule?
options: ATP synthase directly (as its sole component)
questions.correct_answer: Chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Magnesium forms the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, making it essential for photosynthesis; its deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis.

questions.question: Phosphorus is particularly important in plants for its role in:
options: Energy transfer as a component of ATP and nucleic acids
Stomatal opening as the primary osmotic ion
questions.correct_answer: Energy transfer as a component of ATP and nucleic acids
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is a structural component of ATP, ADP, and nucleic acids (DNA/RNA), making it central to energy transfer and genetic material.

questions.question: Photosynthesis in green plants overall converts:
options: Carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy
Glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy
Starch directly into ATP without intermediate steps
questions.correct_answer: Carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy
questions.explanation: The overall photosynthesis equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy to C6H12O6 + 6O2, capturing light energy as chemical energy in glucose.

questions.question: In the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, water is split (photolysis) primarily to:
options: Replace electrons lost from photosystem II and release oxygen as a by-product
Provide carbon for the Calvin cycle
questions.correct_answer: Replace electrons lost from photosystem II and release oxygen as a by-product
questions.explanation: Photolysis of water at photosystem II replenishes electrons removed by light excitation and releases O2 and protons as by-products.

questions.question: The Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) takes place in the:
questions.correct_answer: Stroma of the chloroplast
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle, which fixes CO2 into organic molecules using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, occurs in the stroma, the fluid matrix surrounding the thylakoids.

questions.question: The enzyme RuBisCO catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide onto which five-carbon acceptor molecule?
questions.correct_answer: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)
questions.explanation: RuBisCO catalyses carboxylation of RuBP with CO2 to form two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate, the first step of the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane initially fix carbon dioxide using the enzyme:
options: PEP carboxylase, forming a four-carbon compound
RuBisCO, forming a three-carbon compound directly in mesophyll cells
questions.correct_answer: PEP carboxylase, forming a four-carbon compound
questions.explanation: In C4 photosynthesis, mesophyll cells use PEP carboxylase to fix CO2 into oxaloacetate (a 4-carbon compound), which is later shuttled to bundle sheath cells for the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: Photorespiration in C3 plants occurs mainly because RuBisCO:
options: Can also bind oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, especially under hot, dry conditions with closed stomata
Requires light to catalyse carbon fixation
Works optimally only when CO2 concentration is very low
questions.correct_answer: Can also bind oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, especially under hot, dry conditions with closed stomata
questions.explanation: RuBisCO's oxygenase activity increases when CO2 is scarce and O2 is relatively high (e.g., stomata closed to conserve water), leading to wasteful photorespiration.

questions.question: Cellular respiration in plants overall releases energy by:
options: Oxidising glucose to carbon dioxide and water, generating ATP
Reducing carbon dioxide to glucose using light energy
Converting nitrogen gas into amino acids
questions.correct_answer: Oxidising glucose to carbon dioxide and water, generating ATP
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, releasing stored chemical energy as ATP with CO2 and water as end products.

questions.question: Glycolysis, the first stage of respiration, occurs in the:
questions.correct_answer: Cytoplasm (cytosol)
questions.explanation: Glycolysis, which splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, takes place in the cytosol and does not require oxygen.

questions.question: In the absence of oxygen, plant cells can carry out anaerobic respiration (fermentation), typically producing:
options: Pyruvate and large amounts of ATP
questions.correct_answer: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Under anaerobic conditions, many plant cells ferment pyruvate to ethanol and CO2 (alcoholic fermentation), regenerating NAD+ for continued glycolysis, though yielding far less ATP than aerobic respiration.

questions.question: The respiratory quotient (RQ) of a substrate is defined as the ratio of:
options: Volume of CO2 released to volume of O2 consumed
Volume of O2 consumed to volume of CO2 released
Moles of ATP produced to moles of glucose used
Mass of substrate to mass of water produced
questions.correct_answer: Volume of CO2 released to volume of O2 consumed
questions.explanation: RQ = CO2 evolved / O2 consumed; for carbohydrates it is approximately 1.0, while fats give a lower RQ (~0.7) because they are less oxidised and require more oxygen relative to CO2 produced.

questions.question: Translocation of organic solutes in the phloem is best explained by the:
questions.correct_answer: Pressure-flow (mass flow) hypothesis
questions.explanation: The pressure-flow hypothesis explains phloem translocation as a bulk flow driven by a turgor pressure gradient from source (high solute/high pressure) to sink (low solute/low pressure).

questions.question: In the pressure-flow hypothesis, loading of sucrose into sieve tubes at the source tissue:
options: Lowers the water potential there, causing water to enter osmotically and raise turgor pressure
Directly forces water out of the sieve tube
Has no effect on water potential
Occurs only at the sink end
questions.correct_answer: Lowers the water potential there, causing water to enter osmotically and raise turgor pressure
questions.explanation: Active loading of sucrose into the sieve tube at the source lowers its water potential, drawing water in from the xylem, which raises hydrostatic pressure and drives mass flow toward the sink.

questions.question: Auxins, such as indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), are primarily responsible for:
questions.correct_answer: Cell elongation and apical dominance
questions.explanation: Auxins promote cell elongation (particularly in the shoot) and are largely responsible for suppressing the growth of lateral buds, maintaining apical dominance.

questions.question: Gibberellins are best known for promoting:
options: Stem elongation and breaking of seed/bud dormancy
questions.correct_answer: Stem elongation and breaking of seed/bud dormancy
questions.explanation: Gibberellins stimulate stem internode elongation (famously reversing genetic dwarfism) and help break dormancy in seeds and buds, also inducing enzyme production during germination.

questions.question: Cytokinins primarily promote:
options: Cell division and delay of leaf senescence
questions.correct_answer: Cell division and delay of leaf senescence
questions.explanation: Cytokinins stimulate cytokinesis (cell division) and, in combination with auxin, regulate shoot/root differentiation; they also delay senescence by maintaining chlorophyll and protein levels.

questions.question: Abscisic acid (ABA) is often called a 'stress hormone' because it:
options: Induces stomatal closure and seed dormancy under water-deficit conditions
Promotes rapid stem elongation during flooding
Stimulates cell division at the root tip
Accelerates fruit ripening in climacteric fruits
questions.correct_answer: Induces stomatal closure and seed dormancy under water-deficit conditions
questions.explanation: ABA accumulates under drought stress, triggering guard cells to close stomata to reduce water loss, and it also maintains seed dormancy until conditions favour germination.

questions.question: Ethylene is the plant hormone principally responsible for:
options: Fruit ripening and abscission of leaves/flowers
Breaking of seed dormancy in most species
questions.correct_answer: Fruit ripening and abscission of leaves/flowers
questions.explanation: Ethylene, a gaseous hormone, triggers the ripening process in climacteric fruits and promotes formation of the abscission zone leading to leaf, flower and fruit drop.

questions.question: Phototropism, the bending of a shoot toward light, results from:
options: Asymmetric distribution of auxin causing greater cell elongation on the shaded side
Equal growth on both sides of the stem
Loss of chlorophyll on the illuminated side
Direct movement of the whole plant toward light
questions.correct_answer: Asymmetric distribution of auxin causing greater cell elongation on the shaded side
questions.explanation: Light causes auxin to be redistributed to the shaded side of the shoot, promoting more cell elongation there and causing the shoot to curve toward the light source.

questions.question: Geotropism (gravitropism) in roots, which typically grow downward (positive geotropism), is thought to involve:
options: Sedimentation of starch-containing statoliths that help the root sense gravity
questions.correct_answer: Sedimentation of starch-containing statoliths that help the root sense gravity
questions.explanation: Statoliths (amyloplasts) settle under gravity in root cap columella cells, triggering an auxin redistribution that promotes growth on the upper side and inhibits it on the lower side, curving the root downward.

questions.question: Photoperiodism refers to a plant's physiological response to:
options: The relative length of day and night
questions.correct_answer: The relative length of day and night
questions.explanation: Photoperiodism is the mechanism by which plants (via the pigment phytochrome) detect seasonal changes in day/night length, controlling processes such as flowering.

questions.question: A short-day (long-night) plant will flower when the length of uninterrupted darkness is:
options: Equal to or longer than its critical night length
Shorter than its critical night length
Irrelevant, since only day length matters
questions.correct_answer: Equal to or longer than its critical night length
questions.explanation: Short-day plants actually respond to night length: they flower only when the continuous dark period meets or exceeds a species-specific critical duration.

questions.question: The pigment primarily responsible for detecting red and far-red light in photoperiodic and other light responses is:
questions.correct_answer: Phytochrome
questions.explanation: Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible forms (Pr and Pfr) sensitive to red and far-red light respectively, and mediates photoperiodic timing, seed germination and other light responses.

questions.question: Imbibition, the initial uptake of water by a dry seed during germination, occurs mainly due to:
options: The strong affinity of hydrophilic seed colloids (proteins, starch) for water molecules
Osmosis across an intact semi-permeable membrane only
Root pressure generated by an already-formed root system
questions.correct_answer: The strong affinity of hydrophilic seed colloids (proteins, starch) for water molecules
questions.explanation: Imbibition is a passive physical process in which dry, hydrophilic seed materials absorb water due to matric forces, causing the seed to swell and rupture the seed coat, independent of an established osmotic membrane system.

questions.question: During cereal seed germination, gibberellin released by the embryo stimulates the aleurone layer to synthesise:
options: Alpha-amylase, which breaks down stored starch into sugars
questions.correct_answer: Alpha-amylase, which breaks down stored starch into sugars
questions.explanation: In germinating cereal grains, gibberellin diffuses to the aleurone layer, inducing synthesis and secretion of alpha-amylase, which hydrolyses endosperm starch to provide sugars for the growing embryo.
